These scenarios collectively validate whether modeled data centers exhibit the same vulnerability patterns noted in prior NERC large load loss reviews. 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 5 Challenges and Considerations Modeling large-scale data centers poses significant challenges due to the sheer number of electrical components involved. 5.1 Computational Complexity Simulating this scale with detailed component-level models significantly increases computational time and resource requirements. Each individual device, such as an inverter or a breaker, introduces additional states and equations into the EMT simulation, potentially leading to long run times and memory constraints. 5.2 Model Fidelity vs. Practicality • Detailed modeling involves representing each device with high fidelity. This offers precise insight into fast transients (e.g., inrush currents, dynamic load ramping) and control system interactions, which is critical for the robust evaluation of reliability and protection coordination. • Aggregate modeling simplifies groups of similar devices (e.g., IT loads, BESS, or generators) into lumped equivalent models, reducing the computational burden but potentially losing individual device behaviors and interacting dynamics, which are crucial to assessing certain fast-timescale phenomena. 5.3 Trade-Off Decisions • The need for model accuracy must be balanced with simulation efficiency and the purpose of the study. For system-level studies assessing the overall load impacts or grid interaction, aggregate models might suffice. • Detailed models should be reserved for critical components or subsystems where individual device behavior strongly influences outcomes (e.g., specific IT load or UPS system dynamics affecting grid event studies). • Hybrid approaches combining detailed and aggregated models can effectively target computational resources while retaining sufficient fidelity for key metrics, such as inrush current, load ramp-up profiles, and protection system coordination. Hybrid modeling approaches that combine detailed subsystem representations with aggregated load equivalents provide a practical balance between fidelity and scalability.
